name: Irula
confidence_why: The only statement is a passing parenthetical in Zvelebil 1990 assuming stress on the first syllable inside a historical derivation, Zvelebil 1979 reconstructs second-syllable accent for pre-Irula, and Lal 1991 (Urali dialect) and the Linguistic Survey of India 2023 say nothing about stress, so the placement rests on a guess until Zvelebil 1973 or Perialwar 1979 is read.

catalog_locator: p. 104, section 2.2, ordered rules 1-3 (running head 'ijdl Vol. XIX No. 1 104 Zvelebil'); page image ijdl/archive.org …
catalog_quote: The long voiced occlusive -gg- in Iṟula is most probably to be explained as the result of an assimilative process, not unknown from other Iṟula items. We may set up the following rules: 1. *aṟuku→*öṟugu (vowel centralization because of the following Retroflex) 2. *öṟugu→ *öṟgu (loss of vowel and contraction because of the stress on first syllable) 3. *öṟgu→ öggu (assimilation)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote located and read in (lines 5901-5910) and in the excerpt file; then checked against the page image downloaded from the open archive.org item (bmshri.internationaljou0000visu_h2v5, Servants of Knowledge scan, no login): ijdl/. Verbatim on the page: "1. *aṟuku→*öṟugu (vowel centralization because of the following Retroflex) 2. *öṟugu→ *öṟgu (loss of vowel and contraction because of the stress on first syllable) 3. *öṟgu→ öggu (assimilation)". The stress clause matches the report word for word; minor differences: Zvelebil prints the centralized vowel as ö (report normalizes to ǝ) and arrows → (report uses >). new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word (invoked to explain syncope of the second-syllable vowel in *ǝrugu > ǝggu). Secondary stress not discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Zvelebil 1988 (IJDL 17(1): 157) remarks that accent is 'certainly more important' in Alu Kurumba than in Irula, i.e. stress is of minor importance in Irula.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (the derivation of the single word óggu 'to rot'); the remark is a parenthetical cause in an ordered-rule derivation, not a description of citation-form or phrase stress. Zvelebil's Irula data are Nilgiri Vette Kadu / Mele Nadu Irula. The same author's 1979 footnote (BSOAS 42(2): 367) argues that pre-Irula loss of initial vowels 'can only be explained by strong accentuation of the second syllable' - a historical stage, so not a synchronic contradiction, but it shows accent placement in Irula's history was not stably initial.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement concerns Nilgiri Irula proper (Zvelebil's Vette Kadu / Mele Nadu data; irul1243). The only reachable full grammar, Lal 1991, describes Urali (Ūrāḷi Irula of Coimbatore district, treated by Zvelebil as an Irula dialect and filed by Glottolog under irul1243); it lists five suprasegmental phonemes (two junctures, three terminals) and no stress. The LSI Tamil Nadu 2023 sketch (Udagamandalam Irula) is silent on stress. No Glottolog code separate from irul1243 was found for Urali or Kasaba.

sources.note: Footnote to riddle 34, p. 367: pre-Irula loss of initial vowels 'must point to some rules of accentuation different from those of Tamil-Malayalam.. (in some Kurumba languages one may observe accentuation definitely different from the regular "primary stress on the first syllable")' and 'can only be explained by strong accentuation of the second syllable'; tentative rules *'ale- > *a'le- (change of accent). Historical claim about pre-/proto-Irula, not a synchronic rule.
